items.eventTitle: DOE-UAP-D005, Pantex Unidentified Object Incident Report, 2015
items.title: Pantex ground surveillance radar tracks on aerial imagery
items.description: Aerial satellite image of the Pantex plant area overlaid with a red track line and yellow markers labelled as track points (TP-1 to TP-5) with timestamps around 07:09 to 07:13. Headed "Ground Surveillance Radar Tracks" on page 4 of 6 of the "Pantex Unidentified Object Incident Report". The facility's fenced building complex is visible at upper right and a pond at centre right.

items.eventTitle: DOE-UAP-D005, Pantex Unidentified Object Incident Report, 2015
items.title: Pantex ground surveillance radar tower camera image with object circled
items.description: Grainy camera still headed "Image from Ground Surveillance Radar Tower", showing building rooftops, utility poles and power lines at the bottom with a small dark speck in the sky circled in red at upper right. Page 5 of 6 of the "Pantex Unidentified Object Incident Report", marked UCNI (struck through).

items.eventTitle: DOE-UAP-D005, Pantex Unidentified Object Incident Report, 2015
items.title: Sandia National Labs enhanced images of the Pantex unidentified object
items.description: Two blurred, enhanced images of a dark object on a white background, each showing a darker rounded upper mass with a fainter vertical extension below. Headed "Sandia National Labs Enhanced Images of the Object" on page 6 of 6 of the "Pantex Unidentified Object Incident Report".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Map of reported flying object sightings in the US as of 1 August 1948 (Appendix B)
items.description: Map of the United States and southern Canada, printed sideways, with symbols marking reported sightings concentrated in the Pacific Northwest, California, the Midwest and the East Coast. The inset legend, titled "Reported Sightings of Flying Objects as of 1 August 1948", distinguishes disks, cigar shapes, balls of fire, cones of fire and configuration undetermined. Side heading reads "APPENDIX 'B' — REPORTED SIGHTINGS OF FLYING OBJECTS AS OF 1 AUGUST 1948"; stamped CONFIDENTIAL.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Enlargements of Rhoads flying disk photographs (Figs. 3 and 4)
items.description: Two taped-in photographic enlargements under the heading "ENLARGEMENTS OF ORIGINAL PHOTOGRAPHS": Fig. 3 shows a dark elongated object against a pale sky and Fig. 4 a larger dark crescent or heel-shaped object with a small light spot. Typed text below describes the 10 July 1947 sighting by Pan-American Airways mechanic Mr. Woodruff near Harmon Field, Newfoundland. Page 3 of a SECRET report.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Sky trail through clouds near Harmon Field, Newfoundland (Fig. 5)
items.description: Photograph, mounted sideways on the page, of a cloudy sky with a dark diagonal trail descending from the top, a small dark mark near the centre, power lines, a utility pole and tree tops along the bottom. Labelled "Fig. 5" in the margin with photo number "34923 A.C." at lower right. Associated with the 10 July 1947 Woodruff sighting.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Trail cutting diagonally through cloud bank (Fig. 6)
items.description: Photograph, mounted sideways, showing a thin diagonal trail crossing a bank of cloud beneath a dark sky, with a strip of another image showing water at the right edge. Labelled "Fig. 6" in the margin with an "A.C." photo number at lower right. Accompanies the Harmon Field, Newfoundland trail sighting of July 1947.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Witness sketch of cigar-shaped craft with windows on Henry Grady Hotel letterhead
items.description: Photographic reproduction, shown sideways, of a hand sketch on "HENRY GRADY HOTEL" Atlanta stationery depicting a long segmented cigar-shaped craft with a row of small windows, streamers trailing from one end and a pointed opposite end. Handwritten annotations include an estimated length of "100' in length", a small separate sketch labelled as crew position at upper left, and notes in the lower half. Photo number "A-34919 A.C." appears at upper right.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Witness sketch of windowed craft with flame exhaust on hotel letterhead (Fig. 8)
items.description: Photographic reproduction, shown sideways, of a hand sketch on "HENRY GRADY HOTEL" stationery depicting a rounded, elongated craft with two rows of rectangular windows and a flame-like exhaust streaming from its rear. Annotations include "LARGE WINDOW OR OPENINGS", "100' LENGTH", "NO FINS", a flame-length note, and a circle labelled "ESTIMATED FRONT VIEW ROUND"; a signature appears at lower right. Labelled "Fig. 8" in the margin.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Horten flying wing aircraft on the ground, taped-in print (Fig. 1)
items.description: Taped-in photographic print of a Horten tailless flying wing aircraft resting on the ground in front of a building, viewed along its swept wing. Typed text above notes the Horten 229 twin-jet fighter had reached final stages by the end of World War II and that a Horten glider prototype soared to 14,200 feet as early as 1938. Captioned "Fig. 1"; stamped CONFIDENTIAL.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Horten twin-jet flying wing, rear view of engines (Fig. 2)
items.description: Photograph, printed sideways, of a Horten flying wing aircraft seen from the rear, showing the two jet engine exhausts in the centre section, weathered wing panels and landing gear. Photo number "34918 A.C." along the edge and captioned "Fig. 2" below. Part of a report comparing tailless aircraft to reported flying disks.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Horten flying wing with exposed nose framework and cockpit canopy (Fig. 3)
items.description: Photograph, printed sideways, of a Horten flying wing aircraft on a concrete apron, viewed from the front quarter, showing the cockpit canopy, two jet engine nacelles, landing gear and exposed tubular framework at the nose. Labelled "Fig. 3" in the margin.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Armstrong Whitworth A.W. 52 experimental flying-wing aircraft in flight (Fig. 4)
items.description: Taped-in print of the British Armstrong Whitworth A.W. 52 tailless swept-wing jet in flight over fields, with fins at each wingtip and a label reading "ARMSTRONG WHITWORTH A.W. 52 Experimental Flying-wing Aircraft". Typed text above describes the AW 52 G glider and AW 52 twin-jet and lists specifications (span 90 ft, length 37 ft, 2 Nene II turbo jet units). Captioned "Fig. 4".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Armstrong Whitworth A.W. 52 G glider prototype on grass, March 1945
items.description: Photograph of the A.W. 52 G tailless glider prototype parked on a grass airfield, viewed from behind its large wingtip fin, with roundel markings on the wing and a hangar in the background. Inscription at lower right reads "A.W. 52 G (PROTOTYPE) MARCH 1945 A-32714 A.C.". Part of a report section on British tailless aircraft.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Northrop B-35 flying wing bomber in flight, air-to-air view (Fig. 6)
items.description: Air-to-air photograph of the Northrop B-35 flying wing with its four pusher propellers, flying above a cloud layer, with the engine nacelle of the camera aircraft in the lower right foreground. Labelled "Fig. 6" in the margin with an "A.C." photo number at lower right. Included as an example of US flying wing designs.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Northrop YB-49 jet flying wing in flight over desert terrain
items.description: Aerial photograph of the Northrop YB-49 flying wing viewed from above as it flies over arid terrain, showing its vertical fins, trailing-edge jet exhausts, US star insignia and cockpit canopy. A figure number is typed in the right margin and an "A.C." photo number appears at lower right. Part of a report section on US flying wing aircraft.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Chance-Vought circular-wing "Flying Pancake" aircraft in flight over coastline
items.description: Air-to-air photograph of a Chance-Vought low-aspect-ratio circular-wing aircraft with two large propellers, extended landing gear, twin tail fins and US star insignia, flying above a coastline. Photo number "32964 A.C." at lower right; stamped CONFIDENTIAL in the margin. Accompanies the report's section on the Chance-Vought XF5U-1.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D093, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1948
items.title: Three views of the experimental Arup tailless monoplane (Fig. 9)
items.description: Taped-in composite print of three photographs of the semi-circular-wing Arup tailless monoplane: a side view on the ground, an underside view lettered "THE ARUP INC." with registration "12894", and a front view in flight. The caption reads "Three views of an Experimental Arup tailless Monoplane." with photo number "34924 A.C.". Typed text above quotes Jane's All the World's Aircraft (1935) and gives specifications (span 22 ft, LeBlond engine, 86 mph).

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Map of reported flying object sightings as of 1 August 1948 (Appendix B)
items.description: Photographed map of the United States, shown rotated on the page, with clusters of dot markers indicating reported sightings of flying objects. The page is headed "APPENDIX 'B' — REPORTED SIGHTINGS OF FLYING OBJECTS AS OF 1 AUGUST 1948" and includes a legend strip along the right edge of the map. Part of a 1948 USAF Air Intelligence Report on flying objects.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Rhoads flying object photographs and enlargements, Figs. 1-4
items.description: Four photographs under the headings "ORIGINAL PHOTOGRAPHS BY MR. RHOADS" (Figs. 1 and 2) and "ENLARGEMENTS OF ORIGINAL PHOTOGRAPHS" (Figs. 3 and 4). The originals show a small dark object against the sky, with Fig. 1 bearing the marking "A-34921 A.C."; the enlargements show a dark, elongated, crescent-like silhouette. From a USAF Air Intelligence Report analysing flying disc sightings.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Sky trail photographed near Harmon Field, Newfoundland, 10 July 1947 (Fig. 5)
items.description: Photograph of a cloudy sky with a dark diagonal trail or cleavage through the cloud formation, with a utility pole and tree tops along the bottom edge. The accompanying text describes Pan-American Airways mechanic Mr. Woodruff's report of a circular object leaving a trail that appeared as a "burning up" of the cloud formation, photographed by another PAA employee. Captioned "Fig. 5".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Trail through cloud formation, Harmon Field sighting (Fig. 6)
items.description: Photograph showing a long, thin diagonal trail cutting across a cloud bank, with a strip of a second image (water/shoreline) visible at the right edge. Captioned "Fig. 6", it accompanies the Woodruff sighting near Harmon Field, Newfoundland. Text below summarises other 1947 reports, including Kenneth Arnold's sighting near Tacoma and disks seen from the tanker Ticonderoga.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Witness sketch of cigar-shaped object on Henry Grady Hotel stationery (Fig. 7)
items.description: Photographic reproduction of a hand sketch drawn on "HENRY GRADY HOTEL" letterhead, showing an elongated, segmented cigar-shaped object with lines or streamers trailing from its top end and a pointed lower tip. Handwritten notes appear along both margins and a small separate oval sketch appears at upper right. Captioned "Fig. 7".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Witness sketch of windowed cigar-shaped craft on hotel stationery (Fig. 8)
items.description: Photographic reproduction of a hand sketch on "HENRY GRADY HOTEL" letterhead depicting a rounded, elongated craft with two rows of rectangular windows and multiple vertical streaks emanating from its top. Handwritten annotations run along the sides of the drawing. Captioned "Fig. 8".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Horten flying wing aircraft on the ground (Fig. 1)
items.description: Photograph of a Horten tailless flying wing aircraft parked outdoors in front of a building, viewed from a low angle along the wing. Text above describes the Junkers EF 130, ME 329 and Horten Wing designs, stating the Horten Wing bears "the closest resemblance to the estimated configuration of 'Flying Disks'". Captioned "Fig. 1".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Horten twin-jet flying wing, rear view showing jet engines (Fig. 2)
items.description: Photograph, printed sideways on the page, of a Horten flying wing aircraft seen from behind, showing its two jet engine exhausts set into the centre section and a damaged/weathered wing skin, standing on its landing gear. Captioned "Fig. 2" with a photo number at lower right. Part of a USAF report section comparing foreign tailless aircraft designs to reported "Flying Disks".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Horten flying wing with exposed frame and cockpit canopy (Fig. 3)
items.description: Photograph, printed sideways on the page, of a Horten flying wing aircraft on a runway, viewed from the front quarter, showing the cockpit canopy, engine intakes and partly exposed tubular framework near the nose. Captioned "Fig. 3". From the USAF report's discussion of the Horten Wing as the closest match to the estimated configuration of flying disks.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Armstrong Whitworth A.W. 52 experimental flying-wing aircraft in flight (Fig. 4)
items.description: Photograph of the British Armstrong Whitworth A.W. 52 tailless swept-wing aircraft in flight over patchwork farmland, with fins at the wingtips. A pasted label beside it reads "ARMSTRONG WHITWORTH A.W. 52 Experimental Flying-wing Aircraft". Text above gives specifications (span 90 ft, length 37 ft, 2 Nene II turbo jet units). Captioned "Fig. 4".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Armstrong Whitworth A.W. 52 G glider prototype on grass, March 1945 (Fig. 5)
items.description: Photograph, printed sideways on the page, of the A.W. 52 G tailless glider prototype parked on grass, viewed from behind a large wingtip fin. Inscription in the image reads "A.W. 52 G (PROTOTYPE)" with a March date. Captioned "Fig. 5" in a USAF report section on British tailless aircraft designs.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Northrop B-35 flying wing in flight, air-to-air view (Fig. 6)
items.description: Air-to-air photograph of the Northrop B-35 flying wing bomber seen edge-on with its four propeller engines, flying over water, with part of the camera aircraft's nose visible at upper right. Text above notes it is powered by four reciprocating engines with a 172-foot wing span and a length of only 53 feet. Captioned "Fig. 6".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Northrop YB-49 jet flying wing in flight (Fig. 7)
items.description: Photograph of the Northrop YB-49 flying wing viewed diagonally from above against a light background, showing vertical fins on the trailing edge. Text above describes it as powered by eight turbo-jet engines and the jet-propelled version of the Northrop Flying Wing (B-35). Captioned "Fig. 7".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Chance-Vought XF5U-1 "Flying Pancake" aircraft in flight (Fig. 8)
items.description: Photograph of the circular-planform Chance-Vought XF5U-1 aircraft in flight with its two large propellers and US star insignia on the wing. Text above notes the design is powered by two R-2000-2 engines with a speed range of 40 to 425 miles per hour. Captioned "Fig. 8".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949
items.title: Three views of the experimental Arup tailless monoplane (Fig. 9)
items.description: Composite of three photographs of the semi-circular-wing Arup tailless monoplane: a side view on the ground, an underside view showing the lettering "ARUP" and registration "12894", and a front view in flight. The partially cut caption reads "...ee views of an Experimental Arup tailless Monoplane" and it is labelled "Fig. 9". Accompanying text cites Jane's All the World's Aircraft (1935) and notes unconventional aircraft may explain some flying disk reports.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D096, Correspondence Relating to Project Blue Book, 1955
items.title: Evening Tribune clipping: 'Jerome Teachers, Students Watch Strange Occurrence In The Sky'
items.description: Photocopied front-page clipping from The Evening Tribune, Marysville, Ohio (Vol. 8, No. 42) under the kicker "'Saucer' Experts Stumped". The article reports teachers Mrs. George Dittmar and Rodney Warrick and about 60 pupils at Jerome school seeing a cigar-shaped object and a falling 'angel's hair' substance. Handwritten annotations at top read "This account is correct" and "Yours truly, R. Warrick" with a date.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D096, Correspondence Relating to Project Blue Book, 1955
items.title: Hand-drawn sighting area map near Mexicali showing canals, highway and Cerro Prieto
items.description: Pencil sketch map on lined notebook paper showing roads and waterways near Mexicali. Handwritten labels include "Mexicali City", a highway, a canal with a concrete bridge, an outlined area marked "Cerro Prieto", several "Ejido" plots, and a note reading roughly "15 miles from Mexicali approximately". Arrows trace a travel route along the canal and roads, apparently to locate the reported sighting.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: Compass-rose chart of reported directions of flight of flying objects
items.description: Typed chart titled "REPORTED DIRECTIONS OF FLIGHT" plotting reported object headings along eight compass axes, with arrow ticks along each line and counts at the ends (e.g. NW 63, N 38, S 34, E 22, SE 22, SW 14, NE 9, W 5). A tally at lower left lists "Circling 15, Straight down 3, Direction Indefinite 64, Direction Not Stated 61". A note states that where an undetermined number of objects were reported, the minimum number is plotted, and the same object reported by different people is shown once.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: Photograph of dark flying object against sky with original print inset (Inc 2)
items.description: Enlarged photographic print of a pale sky showing a single dark, irregular leaf-like object with a small light spot near its centre. A small original snapshot is mounted at lower right for comparison. Handwritten "Inc 2" at lower left marks it as an inclosure to the report; stamped CONFIDENTIAL.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: Photograph of two dark objects in sky beside treeline, with original print (Inc 3)
items.description: Enlarged photographic print of a pale sky with dark foliage along the upper right edge, showing a dark elongated object near the bottom left and another dark shape at top left with a thin line extending across the frame. A small original print is mounted at lower right. Handwritten "Inc 3" at lower left; stamped CONFIDENTIAL.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: Highly enlarged grainy image of flying object (Exhibit "A")
items.description: Extreme enlargement of a photographed object showing a grainy, dark teardrop or leaf-shaped form with a light elongated opening near its lower centre. Small "x" marks appear at the object's upper-right tip and lower-left end. Handwritten label "Exhibit 'A'" at lower left; stamped CONFIDENTIAL.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: Horten flying wing aircraft parked outdoors (Inc 5)
items.description: Photograph of a tailless Horten-type flying wing aircraft resting on the ground in front of a building, seen from a low angle along its swept wing. Handwritten "Inc 5" at upper left marks it as an inclosure; stamped CONFIDENTIAL. Included as an example of a conventional tailless design resembling reported flying disks.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: "The Biology of the Flying Saucer—I", The Aeroplane, 13 Feb 1948 (A. R. Weyl)
items.description: Magazine page from The Aeroplane (February 13, 1948, p. 185) with the article "The Biology of the Flying Saucer—I: The Story of Low Aspect Ratio Aircraft" by A. R. Weyl, A.F.R.Ae.S. It includes a photograph of a Chance Vought low-aspect-ratio twin-propeller aircraft, Fig. 1 drawings of the "Turbine flying machine" project of Munich engineer Gustave Koch (1893/1894), and Fig. 2 diagrams defining aspect ratio for aerofoil, pteroid and apteroid shapes. Handwritten "Inc 6" at lower left.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: The Aeroplane, 13 Feb 1948, p.186: annular aerofoils and Kitchen's doughnut (Figs. 3-5)
items.description: Continuation page of A. R. Weyl's flying saucer article in The Aeroplane discussing annular aerodynamics. Illustrations include "Fig. 3.—A simple experiment in annular aerofoils", "Fig. 4.—Principle of the Huth annular-biplane system", and a photograph captioned "Fig. 5. Kitchen's doughnut of 1911" showing an early ring-wing aircraft. Part of the inclosures to a US flying object report.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: The Aeroplane, 13 Feb 1948, p.187: Huth biplane and Cedric Lee monoplane (Figs. 6-7)
items.description: Continuation page of the article on low aspect ratio aircraft in The Aeroplane. It includes line drawings captioned "Fig. 6.—Huth annular biplane of 1909" and "Fig. 7.—Cedric Lee Monoplane No. 1 of Tilghman Richards, 1912", the latter shown in front and plan views. The text recounts early British ring-wing aircraft experiments and ends "(To be continued.)".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: "The Biology of the Flying Saucer—II", The Aeroplane, 5 Mar 1948 (Figs. 8-10)
items.description: Magazine page from The Aeroplane (March 5, 1948, p. 279) with part II of A. R. Weyl's series on low-aspect-ratio aircraft. Line drawings include "Fig. 8.—Project by Warren and Young for a light twin-engined two-seater of 90 h.p. (1937)" in three views, "Fig. 9.—Model of the 'annular wing' of Antes, 1933", and "Fig. 10.—Principle of the Willoughby Delta design". Included as an inclosure to a US flying object report.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: The Aeroplane, 5 Mar 1948, p.280: Delta 8, Hayden glider, Abrial project (Figs. 11-13)
items.description: Continuation page of the flying saucer article in The Aeroplane. It shows "Fig. 11.—Willoughby's 'Delta 8' experimental monoplane of 1938" in plan and side views, a photograph captioned "Fig. 12.—Experimental Hayden glider, 1925" with its dimensions, and "Fig. 13.—A French project of G. Abrial, 1929" in three views. Text discusses disc-wing aerodynamics and early experimenters.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: The Aeroplane, 5 Mar 1948, p.281: parabola glider, NACA Zimmermann tests (Figs. 14-16)
items.description: Magazine page with a photograph captioned "Fig. 14.—A Russian 'parabola' glider of 1924" showing men standing beside the aircraft, a drawing "Fig. 15.—A 'parabola' aircraft by B. I. Tscheranowsky", and a graph "Fig. 16.—N.A.C.A. tests by C. H. Zimmermann which prove the extraordinary stalling qualities of disc wings" plotting lift coefficient against angle of incidence for various aspect ratios. Text covers Zimmermann's research and the stalling behaviour of disc wings.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: The Aeroplane, 5 Mar 1948, p.282: Zimmermann wind-tunnel results graphs (Figs. 17-18)
items.description: Magazine page featuring two aerodynamic graphs: "Fig. 17.—These results from Zimmermann's wind-tunnel tests on disc wings (1932) clearly show the characteristics of low aspect ratio aerofoils", plotting maximum lift, gliding angle and incidence against aspect ratio, and "Fig. 18.—Further results from Zimmermann's tests" plotting lift/drag ratio against aspect ratio for a Clark Y aerofoil section. Text sections include "Pancakes à la Zimmermann" and "An Italian 'Tortellino'"; ends "(To be continued.)".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: "The Biology of the Flying Saucer—III", The Aeroplane, 19 Mar 1948 (Figs. 19-20)
items.description: Magazine page from The Aeroplane (March 19, 1948, p. 337) with part III of A. R. Weyl's series. A photograph is captioned "Fig. 19.—An American 'Flying Flapjack' with two engines. It crashed while under test (1938)." Fig. 20 consists of two plots of lift coefficient against drag coefficient for wings of different aspect ratio, from 1920 Goettingen wind-tunnel results, including a square wing.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: The Aeroplane, 19 Mar 1948, p.338: lift curves and profile drag graphs (Figs. 21-22)
items.description: Magazine page with "Fig. 21.—Lift curves of aerofoils of different aspect ratios", two plots of lift coefficient against angle of incidence from 1920 Goettingen wind-tunnel results, and "Fig. 22.—Increase of profile drag with section thickness, at zero lift" comparing square and rounded tips. Text discusses Zimmermann's work with Chance-Vought, the V-173 and XF5U-1, under the heading "The Real Flying Saucer?".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
items.title: The Aeroplane, 19 Mar 1948, p.339: zero-lift drag vs thickness graph (Fig. 23)
items.description: Magazine page with a graph captioned "Fig. 23.—Increase of zero lift profile drag with thickness ratio of symmetrical aerofoil sections" showing curves and small section sketches for flat plate and other profiles (data from Gerber, Zurich Report No. 6). A small table lists angles of sweep-back against required aspect ratio, from M. B. Morgan. Text discusses German flying wing development and "Hitler's Last Secret Weapon"; ends "(To be continued.)".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: Plots of density and magnitude (size) of an object showing possible relationship
items.description: Hand-plotted graph on graph paper, printed sideways, titled "PLOTS OF DENSITY AND MAGNITUDE (SIZE) OF AN OBJECT SHOWING POSSIBLE RELATIONSHIP". Three side-by-side traces plot two magnitude measurements and a density measurement against film frame number (0 to 100). Stamped CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION; part of a photographic film analysis of an unidentified object.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: Hand-plotted film density/size curves versus frame number (inverted page)
items.description: Graph-paper chart scanned upside down showing two curves, one solid and one dotted, plotted against film frame number from 0 to about 130, with a small legend near the top identifying the two traces. Stamped CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION in the corners. Part of a series of film density analyses of an unidentified object.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: Density readings graph for Montana film, images 1 and 2
items.description: Hand-plotted graph titled "DENSITY READINGS" showing film density for two images (solid and dashed lines) across frames 0 to about 130, with a gap marked "NO IMAGE" in the early frames. A note reads "NOTE — Montana film. Lowest reading indicates brightest image", with a legend for Image 1 and 2 and an enclosure label. Stamped CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: Density readings graph, Phase III Utah film (Enclosure 9)
items.description: Hand-plotted graph titled "DENSITY READINGS" with density values from about 3.4 to 3.8 on the vertical axis and frames 0 to 50 on the horizontal axis, showing a single fluctuating trace with a sharp dip near frame 6 and a dotted section after frame 37. Annotated "NOTE — Phase III Utah Film" and "Enclosure 9". Stamped CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: Density readings graph for four images, smallest reading = brightest (Enclosure 8A)
items.description: Hand-plotted graph titled "DENSITY READINGS" showing four overlaid traces for Images 1-4 across frames 0 to 100, with density values roughly 20 to 30. A note reads "NOTE — Smallest recording indicates brightest image", with a legend for the four images and the label "Enclosure 8A". Stamped CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: Average of density readings, Utah film, four images (Enclosure 10)
items.description: Hand-plotted graph titled "AVERAGE OF DENSITY READINGS" showing four smoothed traces for Images 1-4 plotted against frame number, with values roughly 22 to 31 that dip early and rise toward later frames. Labels include a legend for Images 1-4, "Enclosure 10" and "Note: Utah Film". Stamped CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: Traced motion paths of objects from film (Enclosure 2)
items.description: Tracing on grey paper showing several dotted/irregular motion paths of objects as plotted from film frames, including a long curved arc across the centre, a hooked path at upper right and short fragments below. Labelled "Enclosure 2" in handwriting at lower right. Stamped CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION at top and bottom.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: Plotted motion tracks of multiple objects from film (Enclosure 3)
items.description: Tracing on grey paper showing three clusters of jagged, branching motion tracks running diagonally from upper left toward the centre-right, with short straight reference strokes nearby. Labelled "Enclosure 3" at lower left. Stamped CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION in all four corners.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: Long strip chart of multiple image traces across film frames
items.description: Wide, fold-out graph strip with several groups of solid and dashed traces running left to right, each group labelled by image, with a legend at the far left identifying the line styles. The traces generally rise across the length of the chart, consistent with the density/position plots elsewhere in the film analysis. A faint enclosure label appears at lower left.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: Plotted wavy motion track of object with frame marks
items.description: Tracing on grey paper showing a single horizontal, wavy solid path overlaid with a dashed line and small dot/tick marks along its length, representing the plotted track of an object across film frames. A handwritten enclosure label appears upside down near the top. Stamped CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION in all four corners.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: Hand-plotted object path traces, Enclosure 5B (legend Images 1-5)
items.description: Hand-drawn plot on a stained, partially overlapped sheet showing five path traces rendered in different dashed and dot-dash line styles, one of which rises sharply at the right where the lines converge. A handwritten legend at lower right reads "Enclosure 5B Legend - Image" with line styles keyed 1 through 5. The sheet bears "CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION" stamps (struck through) at top and bottom and is one of the film-analysis enclosures in the document.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: "Relative Image Position within a Group" plot of film image positions
items.description: Large hand-plotted graph titled "Relative Image Position within a Group" showing clusters of small symbols (circles, diamonds, squares, triangles) marking the relative positions of individual images across successive frames, with numbered scale marks along the axes. A dark horizontal band of tape or a fold crosses the middle of the sheet, and a handwritten note and symbol legend ("Legend - Image") sit at lower left beside the label "Enclosure." The sheet carries struck-through "CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION" stamps in each corner.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: Trajectory plot of two images from the "Montana Film," Enclosure 7
items.description: Wide fold-out sheet with two nearly parallel hand-plotted lines (one solid, one dashed) descending gently from upper left to right, representing the paths of two images. A handwritten note at left reads "Note - Montana Film, Enclosure 7" with a legend keying "Image 1" and "Image 2" to the line styles. Struck-through "CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION" stamps appear in all four corners.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D098, Film Analysis of Unidentified Objects, 1953
items.title: "Density Readings" graph of film image density vs. frame number
items.description: Line graph on grid paper titled "DENSITY READINGS" plotting densitometer values (roughly 2.4 to 3.2) against "Frames" numbered 0 to 100, with three overlapping jagged traces. A note at lower right reads "Smallest reading indicating brightest image. Part I" with a legend keying Images 5, 6 and 7, and the sheet is marked "Enclosure 6B." Several struck-through "CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION" stamps cover the chart.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D105, U.S. Air Force Flying Discs File, 1952
items.title: Site sketch of possible UFO investigation area, Arlington, Virginia, 1-2 Sept 1952
items.description: Restricted site sketch titled "Sketch of Area: Investigation of Possible Unidentified Flying Object - Arlington, Virginia - 1-2 Sept. 1952". It shows a large circle about 16 ft across with a 6-inch-wide ring, points marked A and B, a square clothes-line frame at left ("Clothes lines on square frame & central pole") and an "Antenna Wire about 40' above ground" crossing at right. A numbered note identifies a "Small evergreen bush 53" high" inside the circle; the sheet is marked "Incl 2".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D117, AAWSAP DIRD, Metallic Glasses for Aerospace Applications, December 2009
items.title: Figure 1: Amorphous versus crystalline atomic structure of metals (3D renderings)
items.description: Two computer-rendered cubes of packed spheres compare (a) a "Crystalline" lattice with (b) an "Amorphous (glass)" random arrangement. The caption reads "Figure 1. Amorphous Versus Crystalline Structure. Schematic atomic-scale structure of crystalline (a) and amorphous (b) metals." It appears on page 1 of a 'Metallic Glasses' report section on structure.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D117, AAWSAP DIRD, Metallic Glasses for Aerospace Applications, December 2009
items.title: Figure 2: Critical cooling rate charts for metallic glass formation
items.description: Two charts captioned "Figure 2. Critical Cooling Rate." Panel (a) is a temperature-time transformation schematic showing liquid, supercooled liquid, crystal and glass regions, with cooling paths 1-3 between melting and glass transition temperatures. Panel (b) plots critical cooling rate (K/s, log scale) against reduced glass transition temperature, contrasting pure nickel, "Conventional" metallic glasses (thickness < 1 mm) and bulk metallic glasses (> 1 mm), with labeled alloys such as Pd-Cu-Ni-P and Zr-Ti-Cu-Ni-Be.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D117, AAWSAP DIRD, Metallic Glasses for Aerospace Applications, December 2009
items.title: Figure 3: Metallic glass microspring and blow-molded thin-walled bottle
items.description: Two photographs captioned "Figure 3. Examples of Processing of Metallic Glasses." Panel (a) shows a spiral microspring produced by lithography with a 200 µm scale bar; panel (b) shows a thin-walled metallic glass bottle produced by blow molding with a 5 cm scale bar. Images are credited to Professor Jan Schroers (Yale University); the page is part of the 'Casting and Molding' section of a metallic glasses report.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D117, AAWSAP DIRD, Metallic Glasses for Aerospace Applications, December 2009
items.title: Figure 4: Electron micrograph of shear bands in bent zirconium-based metallic glass
items.description: Grayscale scanning electron micrograph of a curved bent specimen edge covered in fine branching shear-band lines, with a 200 µm scale bar. The caption reads "Figure 4. Shear Bands. Produced by bending of a zirconium-based metallic glass." It sits above the report's 'Fracture Toughness' section.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D117, AAWSAP DIRD, Metallic Glasses for Aerospace Applications, December 2009
items.title: Figure 5: Fatigue limit of metallic glasses and metallic-glass-matrix composites
items.description: Log-log plot of stress amplitude/ultimate tensile strength versus number of cycles to failure (10^3 to 10^8). Data series compare a "Single-phase metallic glass" (red circles), a "Dendritic composite" (blue squares) and "High-strength steel" (dashed line), with arrows marking run-outs. Caption: "Figure 5. Fatigue Limit of Metallic Glasses and Metallic-Glass-Matrix Composites", noting zirconium-based glass data and 300-M steel for comparison.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D117, AAWSAP DIRD, Metallic Glasses for Aerospace Applications, December 2009
items.title: Figure 6: Deformation map for metallic glasses (normalized stress vs T/Tg)
items.description: Color-shaded deformation map plotting normalized shear stress τ/µ against temperature normalized to the glass transition (T/Tg), with a secondary axis of shear stress at 300 K (GPa). Regions are labeled "Inhomogeneous deformation (shear localization)", "Elastic (negligible flow)", "Homogeneous deformation", "Non-Newtonian" and "Newtonian", with dashed strain-rate contours from 10^-10 to 1 s^-1. The caption notes values are representative of bulk metallic glass Zr41.2Ti13.8Cu12.5Ni10Be22.5.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D117, AAWSAP DIRD, Metallic Glasses for Aerospace Applications, December 2009
items.title: Figure 7: Cast zirconium-based bulk metallic glass wedge beside a ruler
items.description: Color photograph of a shiny, elongated metallic wedge resting above a Fairgate steel ruler marked in centimeters and inches. Caption: "Figure 7. Cast Metallic Glass Wedge. Wedge of a zirconium-based bulk metallic glass produced by casting. Note the shiny metallic luster, typical of metallic glasses." It introduces the report's section on metallic glass matrix composites.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D117, AAWSAP DIRD, Metallic Glasses for Aerospace Applications, December 2009
items.title: Figure 8: Micrographs of in situ metallic glass matrix composite with dendrites
items.description: Two grayscale scanning electron micrographs captioned "Figure 8. Microstructure of In Situ Metallic Glass Matrix Composite." Panel (a) shows light-gray ductile crystalline dendrites in a dark glassy matrix (50 µm scale bar); panel (b) shows the composite after plastic deformation with multiple slip steps from shear bands interacting with dendrites (10 µm scale bar). The page continues with 'Mechanical Properties of Composites' text and Equation 1.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D117, AAWSAP DIRD, Metallic Glasses for Aerospace Applications, December 2009
items.title: Figure 9: Materials property charts comparing metallic glasses with other materials
items.description: Two Ashby-style bubble charts captioned "Figure 9. Materials Property Charts." Chart (a) plots specific strength against specific stiffness, and chart (b) plots fracture toughness K_Ic against stiffness E (GPa) with dashed contours of equal fracture energy. Metallic glasses (yellow) and dendritic composites (red) are compared with polymers, polymer foams, biologicals, ceramics, crystalline metals, CFRP and GFRP.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D118, AAWSAP DIRD, Aerospace Applications of Programmable Matter, December 2009
items.title: Figure 1: Energy Levels of a Metal and a Semiconductor
items.description: Schematic comparing electron energy levels in a metal and a semiconductor along an "Increasing Energy" axis, with electrons drawn as circled "e-" symbols. The metal side shows electrons moving freely into the "Conduction Band," while the semiconductor side labels a "Valence Band," "Band Gap" and "Conduction Band" with an electron arrow jumping the gap. The caption explains that semiconductors require more energy to excite electrons across the band gap; the page introduces quantum dots in a programmable-matter paper marked UNCLASSIFIED//FOR OFFICIAL USE ONLY.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D118, AAWSAP DIRD, Aerospace Applications of Programmable Matter, December 2009
items.title: Figures 2-3: Quantum Dot barrier structure and Programmable Materials
items.description: Two technical illustrations. "Figure 2. Quantum Dot" shows a block labeled "Barrier" sitting on a larger "Barrier" slab, depicting confinement of electrons in a very small volume. "Figure 3. Programmable Materials" shows a layered device (Conductor, Barrier, Transport Layer, Barrier) with "Confined Electrons" and a voltage source, alongside a fiber cross-section of "Quantum dot particles" surrounding a "Control wire"; the page continues into a section on photonics and metamaterials.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D118, AAWSAP DIRD, Aerospace Applications of Programmable Matter, December 2009
items.title: Figure 4: Wellstone Fiber cross-section with conductor, P/N layers and memory
items.description: Concentric-ring illustration of a notional "Wellstone" fiber, with labels pointing to "Conductors" (yellow segments on the surface), "P-Layer," "N-Layer," "Memory," and a yellow core carrying "Power & Control Signals." The caption describes a flexible cylinder studded with artificial atoms that, when woven, creates a bulk material with programmable properties. The surrounding text discusses future programmable matter and its vulnerabilities to interference and hackers.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D118, AAWSAP DIRD, Aerospace Applications of Programmable Matter, December 2009
items.title: Figure 5: RavenWindow and RavenLight smart window filters in cold and hot states
items.description: Composite of five color photographs showing samples of RavenBrick's thermoreflective window film: a gloved hand holding a tinted film sheet, a framed glass sample, a window filter in front of a soda can, and two pairs of framed panes comparing a city view through clear versus reflective film. The caption reads "Figure 5. Assorted Views of RavenWindow and RavenLight Filters in the Cold (Transparent) and Hot (Reflective) State." The page sits in a section titled "Early Commercialization of Smart Materials" in a document marked UNCLASSIFIED//FOR OFFICIAL USE ONLY.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D118, AAWSAP DIRD, Aerospace Applications of Programmable Matter, December 2009
items.title: Figure 6: Denver five-year cumulative savings, RavenWindow vs. incumbent window filters
items.description: Line chart titled "Denver Five-Year Cumulative Savings (holding energy prices constant)" plotting dollar savings ($0 to $3,000) against "Months Installed" (0 to 60). Seven series are compared: RavenWindow + Low-E (highest, near $2,900), Pilkington K-Glass, Oldcastle Sunglass, Viracon VRE238, AFG Comfort TiR, 99% Transmissive Low-E and 99% Reflective Low-E. The caption reads "Figure 6. RavenWindow Smart Window Film Performance vs. Leading Incumbent Window Filters," followed by text introducing thermal management of spacecraft.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D118, AAWSAP DIRD, Aerospace Applications of Programmable Matter, December 2009
items.title: Figure 7: Peltier Junction Heat Pump schematic
items.description: Schematic of a Peltier junction showing N-Type and P-Type semiconductor blocks bridged by a top "Conductor" labeled "Hot Face" and bottom conductors labeled "Cold Face," with arrows for "Current In" and "Current Out." The caption explains that running current through the device drives thermal energy into the upper conductor, and that the principle also works in reverse to generate voltage. Surrounding text discusses thermoelectric efficiency and using programmable materials to manage heat on spacecraft hulls.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 1: Biomaterial applications in medical devices (photo montage of six implants)
items.description: Six-panel photo montage captioned "Figure 1. Biomaterial Applications in Medical Devices". Panels show a silicone rubber finger joint, a silicone breast implant (shell/filler labels), a polyester and stainless steel heart valve, an X-ray of a titanium hip joint, a polyurethane and metal artificial heart, and a poly(methyl methacrylate) intraocular lens (IOL). It illustrates the introduction to a 'Biomaterials' report.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 3: Polycarbonate, cellulose and silicone biomaterial membranes for sensors
items.description: Color photograph of assorted round white and perforated membrane discs and a perforated sheet laid out on a yellow background. Caption: "Figure 3. Biomaterials Such as Polycarbonates, Cellulose, and Silicones Used in Membranes for Sensors, Dialyzers, and Oxygenators." It accompanies the 'Biomaterials for Biosensors' section.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 4: Silicone (PDMS) breast implants used in reconstructive surgery
items.description: Color photograph of three translucent, purple-lit silicone breast implants on a dark surface. Caption: "Figure 4. Photograph of Silicone (polydimethylsiloxane) Biomedical Implants Used in Breast Reconstructive Surgery." The surrounding text discusses the Dow Corning class-action settlement and the Institute of Medicine review of silicone implants.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 5: Silicone (PDMS) repeating unit chemical structure
items.description: Structural formula of the polydimethylsiloxane repeating unit: an -O-Si- backbone with two CH3 groups on silicon, enclosed in brackets with subscript n. Caption: "Figure 5. Silicone Chemical Groups." It appears in the 'Silicone Chemistry' section of a biomaterials report.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figures 6-7: Silicone foam-cuff tracheostomy tube and silicone scar-repair sheets
items.description: Product photograph labeled "FOAM-CUFF-TRACHESTOMY TUBE" showing a clear tube with green foam cuff and red valve, captioned "Figure 6. Silicone Tracheostomy Tube". Below, two photos show a Mepiform silicone sheet and a woman's face with the sheet applied to the cheek, captioned "Figure 7. Silicone Sheets Used Under the Skin as a Physical Supporting Layer for Repair of Scar Tissue".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 8: Teflon (PTFE) structure, ball-and-stick molecular model and formula
items.description: A rendered ball-and-stick model of a PTFE chain with green fluorine atoms on a carbon backbone, shown beside the structural formula of the repeating -(CF2-CF2)n- unit. Caption: "Figure 8. Teflon Structure." It appears in the 'Teflon' section discussing PTFE and expanded PTFE (Goretex) for medical devices.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figures 9-10: ePTFE lip implant before/after photos and biodegradable PLA mesh
items.description: Two pairs of close-up "BEFORE" and "AFTER" photos of lips, captioned "Figure 9. Expanded PTFE (Gore-Tex or ePTFE) Used in Lip Implants." Below, a photo of a clear twisted lattice-like polymer structure on a blue background is captioned "Figure 10. Biodegradable Polymers. Polymers such as PLA are much like conventional plastics...". The page covers ePTFE cosmetic implants and the 'Biodegradable Polymers' section.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figures 11-12: Polylactic acid molecular model and PLA anti-adhesion barrier illustration
items.description: A rendered space-filling molecular model in green, white and red is captioned "Figure 11. Structure of Polylactic Acid (a Biodegradable Polymer)". Below, an artist's illustration headed "The Clear Choice" shows a hand placing a clear PLA sheet over an exposed heart in an open chest, with the tagline "Protection in case there is a re-operation..." and caption "Figure 12. Biodegradable PLA as an Antiadhesion Barrier after Open-Heart Surgery".

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figures 13-14: PLA/PEG biodegradable polymers graphic and dots of hydrogel
items.description: A promotional graphic reading "PLA/PEG Biodegradable Polymers" over capsule images and faint chemical structures is captioned "Figure 13. Biodegradable Polymers Based on Copolymers of Polylactic Acid and Polyethylene Glycol". Below, a close-up photograph of small translucent droplets is captioned "Figure 14. Dots of Hydrogel". The page covers the polyethylene glycol and hydrogels sections of the biomaterials report.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 15: Titanium components used in hip joint replacement
items.description: Photograph of an assortment of metal hip implant parts, including long femoral stems, ball heads and modular neck pieces, laid on a white surface. Caption: "Figure 15. Various Titanium Components Used in Hip Joint Replacement." It illustrates the 'Titanium - Hip and Knee Joints' section, followed by text on bioceramics.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figures 16-17: Porous hydroxyapatite bone-like structure and bioceramic hip component
items.description: A grayscale close-up of a porous, sponge-like material is captioned "Figure 16. Hydroxyapatite Porous Bone-Like Structure After Commercial Processing". Below, a photo of a white dome-shaped ceramic cup is captioned "Figure 17. Bioceramic Used in Artificial Hip Replacement Component". The text discusses hydroxyapatite and alumina bioceramics.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 18: Computer-based sculpted ceramic teeth (dental crowns)
items.description: Photograph of several natural-looking porcelain dental crowns and a bridge arranged on a white background. Caption: "Figure 18. Computer-Based Sculpted Ceramic Teeth." It appears in the 'Dental Ceramics' section, which describes CAD/CAM-molded dental porcelains and zirconium oxide.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 19: Scaffold-guided tissue regeneration process schematic
items.description: Illustrated left-to-right process flow captioned "Figure 19. Scaffold-Guided Tissue Regeneration". Labeled stages show "Cells" and "Signaling molecules" combined with a "3D matrix", then "Culture" in a dish, then "Implant" into a human leg bone silhouette, and finally "Healty bone" [sic]. It accompanies the report's explanation of tissue engineering with biodegradable scaffolds.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 20: Biodegradable CSLG polymer printed in honeycomb scaffold blocks
items.description: Photograph of two translucent tan cube-shaped polymer scaffolds with a regular grid of pores, shown on a black background. Caption: "Figure 20. Biodegradable Material CSLG Deposited in a Honeycomb Structure to Allow Infiltration by Living Cells While in a Submerged Cell Culture." The text describes ink-jet-like layer deposition of CSLA polymer and introduces 'Cardiovascular Biomaterials'.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 22: Gore Medical Teflon foam vascular grafts (with Figure 21 device table)
items.description: Photograph of several white, ribbed flexible tubes on a blue background, captioned "Figure 22. Gore Medical Teflon Foam Used in Vascular Grafts." Above it, Figure 21 is a text table titled "Medical Devices Used in the Bloodstream" listing devices such as catheters, stents, heart valves and LVADs with their blood contact times. The text notes grafts are made by Gore Medical (Flagstaff, Arizona).

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 23: Illustration of atrial septal defect repair with a Gore Teflon-based patch
items.description: Color medical illustration showing a catheter delivering a disc-shaped Teflon-based occluder patch through a hole in the heart's atrial wall. Caption: "Figure 23. Illustration of Treatment of an Atrial Septal Defect Using a Teflon-Based Product Manufactured by Gore, Inc." The text describes it as an artist's conception of the catheter-inserted patch for infants with septal defects.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figures 24-25: Bjork-Shiley heart valve photo and stent placement illustration
items.description: A photograph of a ring-shaped mechanical valve with a tilting disc is captioned "Figure 24. Stainless Steel and Teflon Bjork Shiley Heart Valve". Below, a medical illustration of an artery cross-section labeled "Dilated balloon catheter and stent", "Stent deployed" and "Plaque" is captioned "Figure 25. Illustration of Stent Placement." The page opens the 'Stent Biomaterials' section.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 26: Nitinol shape-memory alloy stents beside a centimeter ruler
items.description: Photograph of two cylindrical mesh stents, one expanded and one compressed, standing above a ruler marked 2-4 cm. Caption: "Figure 26. Nitinol Stent. Nitinol is an alloy of titanium. It is biocompatible and also a shape memory material." It accompanies the 'Nitinol as a Biomaterial' section, followed by 'Contact Lenses'.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Contact lens on a fingertip (captioned Figure 25: Contact Lens)
items.description: Close-up color photograph of a clear contact lens balanced on a fingertip. Caption: "Figure 25. Contact Lens. Modern contact lenses are made of a mixture of acrylics and silicones that readily pass oxygen to the cornea." The text discusses rigid gas-permeable lenses and introduces 'Drug Delivery Polymers'.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 26: Schematic of biodegradable (bioerodible) drug delivery device
items.description: Schematic showing a large orange sphere labeled "polymer" with embedded dots labeled "drug" at "time - 0", and an arrow to a smaller sphere releasing dots at "time - t". Caption: "Figure 26. Schematic Representation of Biodegradable (Bioerodible) Drug Delivery Device." The text lists localized delivery, sustained delivery and drug stabilization as key advantages.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 27: Photomicrograph of titanium metal integrated with living bone
items.description: Color photomicrograph of pink-stained bone tissue with a scalloped interface against a black region representing titanium. Caption: "Figure 27. Photomicrograph of Titanium Metal (Appears Black in This Photo) in an Intimate Integration With Living Bone. The intersection of the two materials shows a thin barrier layer and then healthy tissue very close to the metal." The text discusses surface treatments and hydroxyapatite coatings for bone integration.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 28: Blood dialyzer illustration (labeled cutaway) and photograph
items.description: Composite figure captioned "Figure 28. Illustration (Left) and Photograph (Right) of a Blood Dialyzer as Used in Medicine." The left line drawing is a cutaway labeled "Blood inlet", "Header", "Tube sheet", "Solution outlet", "Fibers", "Jacket", "Solution inlet" and "Blood outlet"; the right photo shows a cylindrical hollow-fiber dialyzer with red and blue end caps. It appears in the 'Biomaterials in Dialysis' section.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D119, AAWSAP DIRD, Biomaterials, January 2010
items.title: Figure 29: Illustration of Cuprophane dialysis membrane filtering blood waste
items.description: Color illustration of red blood cells on one side of a layered orange-and-yellow membrane, with small violet and orange dots passing through its pores. Caption: "Figure 29. Cuprophane Membrane Passes Blood Waste Products (Violet and Orange Dots) Through Pores and Blocks Passage of Red Blood Cells." The page also contains the report's 'Summary and Recommendations' section.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D120, AAWSAP DIRD, Materials for Advanced Aerospace Platforms, January 2010
items.title: Figure 1: Schematic diagram of friction stir welding (FSW)
items.description: Line-drawn schematic of two plates being joined by a rotating cylindrical tool, with labels "tool rotation", "Tool velocity", "advancing side" and "retreating side" along the weld seam. Caption: "Figure 1. Schematic Diagram of Friction Stir Welding." The text explains FSW for joining high-strength Al alloys such as 7050, including use on the space shuttle external tank.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D120, AAWSAP DIRD, Materials for Advanced Aerospace Platforms, January 2010
items.title: Figure 2: Modified 747 Dreamlifter unloading a Boeing 787 composite fuselage barrel
items.description: Color photograph of a Boeing 747 'Dreamlifter' cargo aircraft with its swing tail open on an airport apron while a large cylindrical fuselage section is unloaded, with ground crew and vehicles around it. Caption: "Figure 2. Specially Modified 747 Transporter Unloading a Boeing 787 Composite Fuselage Barrel Section." It illustrates text on automated tow placement in polymer-matrix composite manufacturing.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D120, AAWSAP DIRD, Materials for Advanced Aerospace Platforms, January 2010
items.title: Figure 3: SEM micrograph of alpha-case phase formation on a titanium alloy surface
items.description: Grayscale scanning electron micrograph (700x, 200 µm scale bar, instrument data strip at bottom) showing needle-like microstructure in grains with an altered surface layer at the right edge. Caption: "Figure 3. Micrograph Showing α Phase Formation at the Surface of a Ti Alloy That has Been Exposed to Air at Elevated Temperature." The text discusses whether alpha case is truly detrimental to Ti alloy sheet structures.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D120, AAWSAP DIRD, Materials for Advanced Aerospace Platforms, January 2010
items.title: Figure 4: Cross-section micrograph of a SiC fiber titanium matrix composite
items.description: Light micrograph showing a dense, regular array of circular fiber cross-sections with small dark centers, with a 1.0 mm scale bar. Caption: "Figure 4. Cross-Section Micrograph of a Ti Matrix Composite." noting C monofilament substrates for SiC deposition, a Ti-6242 matrix and SCS-6 fiber. The text discusses Textron Specialty Materials and SiC fiber availability for TMCs.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 1: Air Force X-25LR Laser Lightcraft depicted in flight over desert
items.description: Color concept image of an acorn-shaped, gold-colored craft hovering above a desert landscape with a bright white plasma glow beneath it and a halo-like ring. Caption: "Figure 1. Air Force X-25LR Laser Lightcraft (courtesy of F. Mead, AFRL/PRSP, Edwards AFB, CA)." The text describes the two-mode laser propulsion concept, with a parabolic afterbody mirror focusing ground-based pulsed laser energy into an annular shroud.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 2: AFRL laser Lightcraft test vehicle in vertical flight
items.description: Color photograph of a spinning, polished conical Lightcraft vehicle against a dark background, with a bright violet-white ring of laser-induced plasma around its shroud. Caption: "Figure 2. AFRL Test Vehicle in Vertical Flight (courtesy of F. Mead, AFRL/PRSP, Edwards AFB, CA)." The rest of the page is blank.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 3: Time-lapse night photo of Lightcraft outdoor vertical flight test
items.description: Night time-lapse photograph showing a dotted vertical streak of light rising from a test site with a crane boom, a domed structure, a small building and a trailer. Caption: "Figure 3. Time-Lapse Photo of a Lightcraft Undergoing an Outdoor Vertical Flight Test (courtesy of F. Mead, AFRL/PRSP, Edwards AFB, CA)."

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figures 4-5: Lightcraft vehicle in horizontal guide-wire flight tests
items.description: Two color photographs. The upper shows a gold, double-cone Lightcraft on a horizontal guide wire, captioned "Figure 4. Lightcraft Flight-Test Vehicle Used in Horizontal Guide-Wire Flight Tests (the top of vehicle is to the right and the laser beam strikes the stretched-out parabolic mirror/propulsion section on the left)". The lower shows the vehicle glowing blue-white during a laser pulse, captioned "Figure 5. Lightcraft Undergoing Horizontal Guide-Wire Flight Test"; both are credited to F. Mead, AFRL/PRSP, Edwards AFB.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 6: Lightcraft undergoing horizontal guide-wire flight test (laboratory still)
items.description: Blurry, blue-tinted video still of a laboratory setup showing the circular rear of a Lightcraft vehicle on a guide wire beside test apparatus. Caption: "Figure 6. Lightcraft Undergoing Horizontal Guide-Wire Flight Test (courtesy of F. Mead, AFRL/PRSP, Edwards AFB, CA)." Below it begins a 'Summary of Technical Performance and Benefits' listing single-stage-to-orbit and launch-cost claims.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 7: Lightcraft nanosatellite concept schematic
items.description: Line drawing of an axisymmetric Lightcraft body with labeled parts: "Shroud (Cowl)", "Forebody: for Lift and Compression of Airflow during Atmospheric Flight", "Afterbody: with Mirrored Surface for Focusing Laser Energy into the Shroud (Cowl)" and "Axi-Symmetric Body". An incoming "Laser Beam" is shown, with notes on laser airbreathing flight to hypersonic speed and laser rocket flight to orbital speed. Caption: "Figure 7. Lightcraft Concept [26]."

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 8: Lightcraft Earth-to-orbit trajectory and associated pointing angles
items.description: Schematic (marked "Not to Scale") of a curved Earth with the "Sensible Atmosphere", a "Ground Based Laser" at "Lightcraft Launch", and the "Lightcraft Earth-to-Orbit Trajectory". Labels mark "End of Laser Airbreathing Propulsion", "End of Laser Rocket Propulsion", "Maximum (Cut-Off) Velocity" and the zenith/vertical. Caption: "Figure 8. Lightcraft Trajectory and Associated Pointing Angles [26]."

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 9: Lightcraft vehicle evolution in three steps (shapes and drag-vs-angle plot)
items.description: Upper drawings show three Lightcraft vehicle outlines labeled (1) "Takeoff Mass = 4.0 kg, Frontal Area = 0.78 m²" and (2)/(3) "Takeoff Mass = 8.0 kg, Frontal Area = .096 m²". Below, a log-scale plot of transonic drag area per unit mass against half-apex angle of forebody (degrees) traces a dashed curve through vehicle shapes with CdA/W values .0026, .0054 and .1658, marking the "SDIO Lightcraft" and a "Range for Currently Envisioned Scramjets". Caption: "Figure 9. Lightcraft Vehicle Evolution (in 3 steps) [26]."

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figures 10-11: Laser beam power attenuation and captured power vs laser wavelength
items.description: Two line graphs plotting fraction of radiated power captured by the Lightcraft against laser wavelength/optimum laser wavelength (0-7). Figure 10, "Attenuation Effects on Captured Laser Beam Power [26]", contrasts beam power attenuation due to diffraction alone with diffraction plus atmospheric effects. Figure 11, "Influence of Trajectory and Laser Wavelength on Captured Power [26]", compares the Earth-to-orbit trajectory, end of laser airbreathing propulsion, and end of airbreathing and rocket propulsion.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 12: Captured laser power vs range from 11.2 µm CO2 laser
items.description: Log-scale graph of laser power captured by the Lightcraft (W, 1E+04 to 1E+07) against Lightcraft slant range from laser (0-500 km) for an "11.2 micron Laser Wavelength". Curves compare laser beam angles of 0° and 83° from the vertical, plus a "No Adaptive Optics" case. Caption: "Figure 12. Captured Laser Power vs. Increasing Range from 11.2 µm CO2 Laser [26]."

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 13: Influence of Lightcraft range and pointing angles on captured power
items.description: Graph of laser power captured by the Lightcraft (MW, 0-6) against slant range from laser (100-500 km) for "Radiated Laser Power = 10 MW", comparing 1.62 micron and 11.2 micron laser wavelengths. Annotations mark beam angles from 50° to 83° from the vertical, "End of Laser Airbreathing Propulsion", "Lightcraft Capture Dia. of 30 cm" and "Lightcraft Achievement of Orbital Speed" (2.9 MW and .04 MW endpoints). Caption: "Figure 13. Influence of Lightcraft Range and Pointing Angles on Captured Power [26]."

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 14: Ground/sea-to-space laser Lightcraft concept (Earth-to-orbit)
items.description: Simple schematic titled "Ground-to-Space (Earth-to-Orbit)" showing a laser beam rising from Earth's curved surface to a small Lightcraft, which follows a dashed ascent path labeled "Pico or Nano Satellites". Caption: "Figure 14. Ground/Sea-to-Space Concept: Appropriate rotation of a high-energy laser beam, emanating from a ground/sea-based laser, guides and propels an integral Lightcraft pico-/nano-satellite along an ETO ascent path..." It opens 'Chapter 3: Laser Lightcraft Weapon Mission Selection Study'.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 15: Air-to-space laser Lightcraft concept against ballistic missiles
items.description: Schematic titled "Air-to-Space (Ballistic Threats)" showing an "Air Launch: H ~ 12 km, V ~ M 0.8" aircraft beaming a laser to a Lightcraft on a dashed path toward "Enemy Ballistic Missiles" above Earth's curve. Caption: "Figure 15. Air-to-Space Concept: Appropriate rotation and translation of a high-energy laser beam, emanating from a moving aircraft, guides and propels a Lightcraft toward a nearly head-on collision with an incoming ballistic missile..." The page continues with assumed laser and trajectory limitations.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 16: Schematic of power oscillator optics for a high-power laser
items.description: Schematic of a laser cavity showing end mirrors M1 and M2, an acoustic muffler "AM", an "E-Gun" and an output scraper "SP" along a dashed optical axis. A legend lists "End Mirrors: M1 Concave (R1 =97m), M2 Convex (R2=24m)", "Magnification: M=4", output scraper dimensions, "Cavity Length: 36.5m", "Gain Length: 3m" and "Aperture: 0.3x0.3 m". Caption: "Figure 16. Schematic of Power Oscillator Optics [29]."

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 17 MOPA laser schematic and Figure 18 N2/CO2/H2 laser gas flow system
items.description: Two technical schematics. Figure 17, "Schematic of MOPA," shows a master oscillator and power amplifier with electron guns, acoustic mufflers, end mirrors M1/M2, turning flat M3, optical isolator, output scraper and beam expansion optics, with a labelled key. Figure 18, "Schematic of the Laser N2/CO2/H2 Gas Flow System," traces gas from a primary storage tank through a flow control valve, screen, sonic orifice and plenum chamber to the gain cell and gas exit horn, with listed gas pressures (P1 = 150 Atm) and mixture parameters (N2:CO2:H2 3:1:0.08).

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 19: Northrop Grumman Joint High Power Bulk Slab Solid-State Laser in lab
items.description: Photograph of a technician in a cleanroom suit, hood and goggles working over an optical bench crowded with mirrors, mounts and amplifier modules. Captioned "Figure 19. Northrop Grumman's Joint High Power Bulk Slab Solid-State Laser (courtesy of the Directed Energy Professional Society)." It appears in a section on emergent high-power solid-state and free-electron laser technologies, describing the JHPSSL 7-amplifier chain that reached about 105 kW in 2009.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 20: rendering of DARPA High Energy Liquid Laser Area Defense System (HELLADS)
items.description: Computer-generated 3D rendering of a modular laser assembly: rows of stacked grey, blue and yellow modules mounted on a long black base, with a translucent green beam path and red/pink optical housing at one end. Captioned "Figure 20. DARPA's High Energy Liquid Laser Area Defense System (courtesy of P. Saunders, AFRL/RDS, Kirtland AFB, NM)." The surrounding text lists characteristics and technical features of bulk solid-state lasers.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 21: phase change material heat storage module for directed-energy lasers
items.description: Photograph of a flat rectangular metal plate module with copper-coloured edges held between two threaded rods on a grey background. Captioned "Figure 21. Phase Change Materials Allow Storage of Large Intermittent Heat Loads While Slow Regeneration Removes Heat from Aircraft (courtesy of P. Saunders, AFRL/RDS, Kirtland AFB, NM)." The text discusses a 3 MJ thermal energy storage device for cooling directed-energy weapon systems, followed by the start of a section on high-power fiber lasers.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figures 22-23: HPFL MOPA design and fiber laser beam combining techniques
items.description: Figure 22, "Typical HPFL MOPA Design," shows a master oscillator feeding a (6+1) to 1 combiner with fiber-coupled pump modules, doped double-clad gain fiber and a high-power endcap. Figure 23, "Fiber Laser Beam Combining Techniques," is a slide titled "State of the Art in Fiber Combining" with six panels: passive phasing, coherent beam combining (CBC), incoherent beam combining with a hexagonal beam director, Talbot self-imaging coupling, spectral beam combining with a grating, and MOPA with active phase control. Both are credited to the Directed Energy Professional Society.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figures 24-25: pumping fiber lasers and large vs small diameter fiber lasers
items.description: Figure 24, "Pumping Fiber Lasers," depicts pump fibers (yellow) bundled into a blue fiber with a highly reflective grating, low index polymer and output coupler grating, plus inset cross-sections of fiber bundles. Figure 25, "Large and Small Diameter Fiber Lasers," shows laser pump diodes feeding an active fiber (side view) with ray paths, an end view of seven pump fibers around an active fiber, and a note on total internal reflection angle setting divergence and beam quality. Both are credited to the Directed Energy Professional Society.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figures 26-27: IPG Photonics single-mode fiber laser modules and 50 kW multimode HPFL
items.description: Figure 26, "Single Mode Fiber Laser Modules," combines photos of compact laser modules (open chassis with fiber coils and a sealed unit) with specs including POUT up to 1,100 W, wavelength 1070 nm and weight ~12 kg. Figure 27, "Multimode HPFLs," shows a photo of a large multi-cabinet 50kW multimode fiber laser installation beside a bullet list of specs (DC EOE ~33%, weight ~2,500 kg, delivered August 2008). Images are credited to IPG Photonics and illustrate portable industrial high-power fiber lasers.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figures 28-29: free-electron laser undulator illustration and FEL mechanism
items.description: Figure 28, "Free-Electron Laser," is a 3D illustration of an electron beam passing through an undulator of alternating N/S magnets, with a red-boxed close-up of the wiggling electron path and an orange output laser beam. Figure 29, "Free-Electron Laser Mechanism," schematically shows electron beam pulses passing through a wiggler between a "100 % reflecting mirror" and a "partially transmitting mirror," with photon emission producing optical laser pulses. Both are credited to the Naval Post-Graduate School FEL Lab and accompany text explaining how FELs generate coherent light.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 30: free-electron laser electron beam phase-space evolution
items.description: Diagram of an electron beam passing through an undulator between a resonator mirror pair, above three phase-space plots (gamma vs. z, 0 to lambda) showing the electron distribution progressively bunching into red/orange curves. Labelled "electron beam phase-space evolution" and captioned "Figure 30. Free-Electron Laser Electron Beam Phase-Space Evolution (courtesy of the Naval Post-Graduate School FEL Lab)." The following text explains electron bunching and lists benefits of FELs.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 31: recirculating-beam free-electron laser (RBFEL) system schematic
items.description: Schematic of a recirculating-beam FEL showing an electron accelerator of cavity cells atop a central "RF Power Liquid Helium Refrigerator" block, with a beam dump and injector on either side and a red dotted electron beam loop. Below, a resonator line runs from a reflecting mirror through a green undulator to an out-coupling mirror. Captioned "Figure 31. Recirculating-Beam FEL System (courtesy of the Naval Post-Graduate School FEL Lab)," in a passage on the Navy DE&EWS program and RBFEL technical features.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 32: high-power FEL optical resonator dimensions
items.description: Simple line diagram of an optical resonator: two curved mirrors separated by S=16m, with a green undulator element of length L=0.6m at the centre and beam dimensions w=2.6cm, Z0=2cm and w0=0.1mm marked on the converging blue beam lines. Captioned "Figure 32. High-Power FEL Optical Resonator (courtesy of the Naval Post-Graduate School FEL Lab)." The page continues with estimated payload costs for Lightcraft launch using 10 MW laser systems.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 33: notional long-range HEL beam control system
items.description: Block-and-ray diagram divided into Laser, Beam Control and Lethality sections, tracing a beam from a laser device module through deformable mirrors, alignment sensor, target-loop and local-loop wavefront sensors, and an illuminator telescope on an inertial platform, through the atmosphere to a missile target. Laser types listed: chemical, solid-state, free-electron. Captioned "Figure 33. Notional Long Range HEL Beam Control System (courtesy of the Directed Energy Professional Society)," following a bullet list of key features of a new HEL beam control architecture.

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 34: inertially stabilized HEL beam pointer/tracker mount with turret photo
items.description: Slide titled "Inertially Stabilized Pointer/Tracker Mount" diagramming a gimbal with tracker, stabilization electronics, mount drive, gyro and beam expander, with angles theta-sensor, theta-error, theta-target and theta-HEL pointing toward a rocket. An inset photo shows a spherical beam-director turret, and a note reads "To achieve the high precision required for a HEL Weapon, The sensor and Beam Expander must maintain precise alignment." Captioned "Figure 34. HEL Beam Pointer/Tracker (courtesy of the Directed Energy Professional Society)."

items.eventTitle: DOW-UAP-D143, AAWSAP DIRD, Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites, November 2010
items.title: Figure 35: basic shared aperture beam control system (TILL, C4I)
